rationale: Neuroimaging findings across the NFU1 phenotypic spectrum support the hypothesis that cystic and cavitating leukoencephalopathy is severity- and age-dependent rather than an obligate feature of NFU1-related spastic paraplegia (SPG93). While classic severe infantile forms (such as MMDS1) and early relapsing cases characteristically display cystic degeneration and cavitation, milder and later-onset spastic paraplegia presentations often demonstrate non-cavitating white matter abnormalities or less prominent changes. Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022) and Tonduti et al. (2015) demonstrate that white matter involvement is invariable, but the specific finding of cavitating leukoencephalopathy is non-obligate in slowly evolving, milder HSP phenotypes.

evidence.text: In a study of 19 individuals across 10 families harboring bi-allelic NFU1 variants displaying an early-onset pure to complex hereditary spastic paraplegia continuum, white matter abnormalities on neuroimaging were invariable, spanning from severe cavitating leukoencephalopathy at one extreme to complex HSP with prolonged survival.

source.title: New spastic paraplegia phenotype associated to mutation of NFU1
source.quote: We report a new NFU1 mutated patient presenting with a milder phenotype characterized by a later onset, a slowly progressive spastic paraparesis with relapsing-remitting episodes, mild cognitive impairment and a long survival. The early white matter abnormalities observed on MRI was combined with a mixed sensory-motor neuropathy in the third decade.

evidence.text: A 27-month-old girl with homozygous NFU1 mutation presenting as spastic paraparesis mimicking cerebral palsy showed hyperintensity of cerebral white matter prominent in frontal regions with partial cystic degeneration and cavitation.

source.quote: Magnetic resonance imaging revealed hyperintensity of the cerebral white matter that was more prominent in the frontal regions, with milder involvement in the posterior periventricular regions. There was also evidence of partial cystic degeneration and cavitation in the frontal regions.
